finding.claim: The DELETE /reports/:id handler calls the async authorize() without await. A failed authorization check rejects a promise that nothing handles, and execution continues to db.reports.remove(). Any authenticated user can delete any report, including ones they have no 'delete' grant on. The unhandled rejection can also terminate the process on Node 15+ (default unhandled-rejections=throw), which gives a secondary denial of service.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sends DELETE /reports/<id> for a report they have no 'delete' grant on. The id comes from req.params.id.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: The report is fetched by the attacker-supplied id.
authorize(...) is called without await or .catch. The returned promise is discarded.
The grants lookup is asynchronous. When the grant is missing, the thrown 403 only rejects the discarded promise.
db.reports.remove runs regardless of the authorization result.
The handler returns 204, so the attacker sees success.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() would throw on a missing grant, but its result is never awaited, so it has no effect. The PUT handler at line 27 does await it, which confirms the intent and that DELETE is the outlier. No other middleware or route-level authorization is present. The only global middleware at line 4 just copies req.session.user and does no permission check. There is no error-handling middleware or try/catch around the call.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws 403 on a missing grant, but the DELETE handler at line 20 calls it without await or .catch. The global middleware at line 4 only copies req.session.user. There is no error middleware and no try/catch.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() without await, so the 403 thrown at server.js:14 only rejects a discarded promise. server.js:21 then runs db.reports.remove and line 22 returns 204 to any authenticated user. The PUT handler at line 27 does await it.
